sec.title: Background
sec.p: Colorectal carcinoma exhibits high heterogeneity, comprising subtypes that show poor efficacy of T cell-based immunotherapies, such as programmed cell death protein 1 (PD-1) checkpoint inhibitors. Although natural killer (NK) cells are considered a promising approach for cancer immunotherapy, it remains unclear what molecular mechanisms drive NK cell activation or suppression within the tumor microenvironment. Moreover, limitations in human tumor models that reflect the diversity of individual patient tumors hinder the ability to effectively select patients who would benefit most from NK cell-based therapies.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: Here, we established a co-culture platform of genetically diverse colorectal cancer (CRC) patient-derived organoids (PDOs) with primary allogeneic NK cells. We performed bulk RNA sequencing analysis of sorted NK cells after exposure to PDOs and aligned gene expression signatures derived from our findings with publicly available single-cell RNA sequencing data of NK cells from peripheral blood and CRC tissues of patients. Moreover, we evaluated identified pathways using flow cytometry and IncuCyte live-cell imaging analysis to quantify phenotypic alterations and NK cell-mediated killing of PDOs over time, respectively. Ultimately, we tested CRISPR-Cas9-edited NK cells and PDOs, small molecule compounds, and clinically relevant monoclonal antibodies (mAbs) to increase NK cell potency.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: On co-culture, NK cells acquired common transcriptional signatures related to hypoxia and transforming growth factor-beta (TGF-β), similar to NK cells infiltrating CRC tissues of patients. In addition, we observed patient-specific differential PDO susceptibilities to NK cell-mediated lysis. Major histocompatibility complex class I deficiency and natural killer group 2, member D (NKG2D)-ligand expression on PDOs facilitated NK cell-mediated cytotoxicity, and induced phenotypic NK cell diversification related to activation and the acquisition of inflammation and tissue-residency-related transcriptional signatures. Genetic or pharmaceutical targeting of hypoxia-inducible factors HIF1A/EPAS1 or TGF-βR1, or the addition of anti-CEACAM1 mAbs, enhanced NK cell-mediated PDO killing or activation, respectively.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: The NK cell/PDO co-culture platform allows the identification of both common and patient-specific impacts of the tumor microenvironment on NK cell function and can aid the development of patient-tailored immunotherapies. The majority of CRC (CMS2/CMS3) PDOs from our cohort were susceptible to NK cell-mediated killing and induced NK cell activation, highlighting the potential of NK cells for CRC immunotherapies.
Keywords: Tumor Microenvironment, Colorectal Cancer, Natural killer - NK

caption.title: WHAT IS ALREADY KNOWN ON THIS TOPIC

list-item.p: We established a platform recapitulating the reciprocal interactions of colorectal cancer PDOs and allogeneic human primary NK cells, unveiling the PDO-specific characteristics (natural killer group 2, member D (NKG2D)-ligandhigh, major histocompatibility complex class 1low) conveying susceptibility to NK cell-mediated killing and diversification related to NK cell activation. Furthermore, we demonstrated both common and PDO-specific NK cell adaptations on co-culture with NK cell-susceptible and NK cell-resistant PDOs. Through genetic or pharmaceutical targeting, we could overcome the hypoxia-mediated and transforming growth factor-beta (TGF-β)-mediated immunosuppressive organoid microenvironments and further increase NK cell cytotoxicity.

sec.title: HOW THIS STUDY MIGHT AFFECT RESEARCH, PRACTICE OR POLICY

list-item.p: Our platform can be leveraged not only for target identification, but also for patient-tailored preclinical testing and screenings of innovative immunotherapeutic treatments and for selection of patients who would benefit most from NK cell-based therapies. Therapeutic approaches counteracting immunosuppression by hypoxia and TGF-β1 could be of high relevance to increase the efficiency of adoptively transferred allogeneic NK cell products against solid tumors in the clinics.

sec.title: Background
sec.p: Although the immunotherapy of cancer against hematologic malignancies has yielded impressive results, the benefits of immunotherapies for patients with solid tumors remain limited.1 Colorectal cancer (CRC) is one of the most frequent cancer types, and treatment options are poor if diagnosed at late stages.2 CRCs are subclassified into four consensus molecular subtypes (CMS), characterized by varying degrees of genetic instability, stromal recruitment, and metabolic dysregulation.3 While CMS2 is generally associated with low immunogenicity and a “cold” tumor microenvironment (TME), CMS3 is considered more immunogenic, yet still lower when compared with CMS1.3 CMS4 exhibits an “immune-excluded” phenotype driven by extensive stromal remodeling and enrichment of cancer-associated fibroblasts.3 The high stromal dependency of this subtype is also reflected in vitro, as CMS4-derived organoids require stromal cues for sustained growth and viability.4 CMS2 and CMS3 are predominantly microsatellite stable, resulting in a low mutational burden and limited neoantigen formation associated with rather poor efficacy of T cell-based immunotherapies, such as programmed cell death protein-1 checkpoint inhibitors.5 Hence, there is an urgent need for the development of alternative therapies involving immune cell types that are independent of the presence of tumor neoantigens. Even within individual patient tumors, there is considerable heterogeneity among CMS subtypes,6 underlining the necessity to develop personalized treatment options.

Natural killer (NK) cells are innate cytotoxic lymphocytes that contribute to the first line of defense against viral infections and tumors.7 8 Their activation is mediated by balanced signals delivered downstream of activating and inhibitory receptors expressed on their cell surface.9 10 Activating receptors, including natural cytotoxicity receptors (NCRs) and natural killer group 2, member D (NKG2D), recognize stress-induced and malignancy-induced ligands, mediate target cell lysis, and the production of inflammatory cytokines.11 12 Inhibitory receptors include killer-cell immunoglobulin-like receptors (KIRs), which recognize self-major histocompatibility complex (MHC) class I molecules.13 Due to their high cytotoxic potential and the favorable safety profile, there is emerging interest in using NK cells as therapeutic agents.8 14 Classically, NK cells are considered to circulate within the blood stream, where they constitute 3–10% of peripheral blood lymphocytes. On entry from the circulation into solid tumors, NK cells encounter a patient-specific set of tumor-expressed ligands for inhibitory/activating receptors that affect the susceptibility to NK cell-mediated lysis.15 Moreover, within solid tumors, NK cells become exposed to a hostile microenvironment that shapes their reactivity.15 16 Accordingly, NK cells derived from patients’ CRC tissue displayed downregulated activating and upregulated inhibitory receptors and impaired functionality.17 18 Adaptation of NK cells to limited oxygen availability—a common feature of solid tumors—results in the stabilization of hypoxia-inducible (transcription) factors (HIFs) that coordinate cell metabolism, proliferation, and effector functions.19,21 Other suppressive features of the TME include soluble molecules that can impair immune cell reactivity, such as transforming growth factor-beta (TGF-β).22 23 The sets of tumor-expressed NK cell ligands and the tumor microenvironmental factors that determine the susceptibility of tumors of individual patients with CRC to NK cell lysis are still poorly defined.

There is increasing evidence from studies in solid tumor models24 and in xenograft models25 that after initial cell activation, NK cell subsets can develop programs of cell dysfunction. Thus, the intratumoral NK cell compartment is characterized by a phenotypic and functional heterogeneity. Previous studies in tumor mouse models26 and in patients with cancer27,30 revealed that intratumoral NK cells exhibit a diverse spectrum of phenotypes related to cytotoxicity, cytokine and chemokine production, alongside expression of the integrin CD49a,26 a marker for activated and tissue-resident immune cells.31 32 Since NK cells are scarce in CRC tissue,33 functional evaluations of these signatures are challenging. A better understanding of the features driving NK cell functional diversification in solid tumors could have high relevance for the design of NK cell-based cell therapy protocols for patients with cancer. For patients with CRC, so far, clinical benefits of allogeneic NK cell infusions remained limited.34 Shortcomings of human model systems that reflect patient-specific tumor characteristics hamper the pre-selection of patients with high probability to respond to NK cell therapies.

In this work, we established a platform of well-characterized CRC patient-derived organoids (PDOs) to model features of the individual patients’ TME35 and identified differential susceptibilities of patient-derived CRC organoids to NK cell-mediated killing. We uncovered features common to PDOs encountered by NK cells, including hypoxia and TGF-β. We also identified patient-specific features of PDOs such as the induction of NK cell diversification related to activation and of tissue-residency-like traits highlighting the applicability of our platform for testing personalized immunotherapeutic interventions.

sec.title: Human primary NK cell isolation and culture
sec.p: Human primary NK cells were isolated from healthy donors’ buffy coats obtained from the blood bank of the DRK-Blutspendedienst Baden-Württemberg-Hessen (Mannheim, Germany) under sterile conditions. Peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) were isolated by gradient centrifugation (Biocoll, Separating Solution, Biochrom), and NK cells were purified from PBMCs using the human NK cell isolation kit (Miltenyi), yielding a purity of 94.4% CD56+ CD3− CD14− CD19− cells and less than 1.09% T cell (CD3+) contamination (n=23) as determined by flow cytometric analysis (data not shown). NK cells were cultured at a concentration of 2 million/mL in complete NK cell medium (Miltenyi), supplemented with 10% human serum (PAN), 100 U/mL penicillin/streptomycin (P/S) (Gibco), and 400 U/mL recombinant human interleukin (IL)-2 (National Institutes of Health (NIH)).

sec.title: Patient-derived organoid culture
sec.p: The generation of CRC PDOs was previously described.36 Only untreated patients with a new diagnosis of colon or rectal cancer were included in this study (online supplemental table 1), while patients with active HIV, hepatitis B virus (HBV), orhepatitis C virus (HCV) infections were excluded. The selection bias of patients was minimized as much as possible; however, as the study population was recruited from a single center, there was an enrichment for Caucasians. Eight PDO cell lines were used: PDO7, PDO13, PDO19, PDO22, PDO30, PDO46, PDO324, and PDO330 (randomized by number). PDOs were cultured in basement membrane extract domes (BME, R&D Systems) and in PDO medium as previously described.37 After 4–5 days of culture, the medium was replaced with PDO medium without the apoptosis inhibitor Y-27632 (Biomol). After 7–8 days, PDOs were washed with phosphate-buffered saline (PBS), digested with TrypLE Express Enzyme (Thermo Fisher) at 37°C to obtain single-cell solutions, counted, and re-seeded.

sec.title: NK cell/PDO co-cultures
sec.p: For NK cell/PDO co-cultures, we used PDOs 5–7 days after splitting. PDOs were washed with PBS, and excessive BME was dissolved using non-enzymatic cell recovery solution (Corning) two times for 10–15 min on ice. Afterward, a fraction (1/6 to 1/8) of the total PDOs was digested as described above, and single-cell PDOs were counted to calculate the cell numbers of the undigested three-dimensional (3D) organoid fraction. 2-day IL-2-stimulated NK cells were digested using Accutase (Merck) for 7 min at 37°C, washed with Roswell Park Memorial Institute (RPMI) (+10% human serum and 100 U/mL P/S), and counted. NK cells and PDOs were added to ultra-low attachment tubes (Corning) in an effector to target (E:T) ratio of 0.375:1, spun down, and the excessive supernatant was carefully removed. For NK cell/PDO co-cultures, cells were resuspended in BME, and six BME domes (each 3–4 µL) were seeded in 24-well cell culture plates. After incubation for 30 min at 37°C, a 1:1 mixture of the PDO medium37 without Nicotinamide (Sigma-Aldrich)38 and Y-27632, and RPMI supplemented with 10% fetal calf serum (FCS), 100 U/mL P/S, and 100 U IL-2 was added. NK cell/PDO co-cultures were cultured for 4 days at 37°C and in 21% O2. For comparisons of NK cell/PDO co-cultures under hypoxic and normoxic conditions, cells were cultured for 4 days in an incubator mimicking either hypoxia (1% O₂) or normoxia (21% O₂).

For the comparison of PDOs cultured in two-dimensional (2D) (single cells) or 3D, the same number of cells were seeded; however, the 2D organoid fractions were previously digested as described above. For the experiments inhibiting TGF-βR1, A-83 (Sigma) was removed from the NK cell/PDO co-culture medium, and galunisertib (10 µM, MedChemExpress) was added as indicated. For the co-cultures with NK cells in tissue culture inserts (0.4 µm, Sarstedt), PDOs were seeded in BME domes on the bottom, and NK cells were added to tissue culture inserts or co-seeded with PDOs in BME domes. For co-cultures containing monoclonal antibodies (mAbs), NK cells and PDOs were prepared in 15 mL reaction tubes, as described above, with E:T ratios ranging from 0.2 to 0.375:1, and spun down. After removing the supernatant, the remaining cells were resuspended in BME and filled up with co-culture medium, thereby creating a 5% BME low-viscosity suspension culture. Antibodies (anti-NKG2D, clone: 1D11, 11 µg/mL, BioLegend and anti-CEACAM1, clone: CM-24, 1 µg/mL, Bio-Techne) were added after cell seeding for 4 days.

sec.title: Flow cytometry analysis and cell sorting
sec.p: For flow cytometry analysis, cells were harvested, washed with PBS, and digested as described above. Cells analyzed by flow cytometry were stained with ZombieAqua Fixable Viability Kit (BioLegend) to identify apoptotic cells. Cells separated by cell sorting were stained with 7‑aminoactinomycin D (7-AAD) (BD) to exclude apoptotic cells. TruStain (BioLegend) was added to block unspecific binding to Fc receptors prior to staining with mAbs. Cells were stained with primary mAbs for 30 min at 4°C. For staining of chemokine receptors, mAbs were added to the cells and incubated at 37°C for 10 min. Afterward, the other mAbs were added and cells were incubated at room temperature (RT) for 20 min. All mAbs used are listed in (online supplemental table 2). Flow cytometry was performed with LSRFortessa (BD) and cell sorting with FACSAria Fusion (BD). Flow cytometry data were processed with the FlowJo software (V.10.9.0). For the t-distributed stochastic neighbor embedding (t-SNE) representation of NK cell markers, NK cells only, and NK cells from PDO co-cultures were gated for live CD56+ cells, downsampled to 4,000 cells, concatenated, and finally, the FlowJo t-SNE tool was run with predefined settings.

sec.title: IncuCyte live-cell imaging and analysis
sec.p: PDO only or PDO/NK cell co-cultures were prepared as described above, seeded in 3 µL BME domes, and placed in the center of flat-bottom 96-well cell culture plates. After 30 min at 37°C, 200 µL of co-culture medium was added, and cell culture plates were placed in an SX5 IncuCyte system (Sartorius). For cytotoxicity assays, Cytotox Red dye (125 nM, Sartorius) was added. To visualize hypoxic areas (oxygen concentration <5% O2), Image-iT hypoxia green dye (2 µM, Thermo Fisher) was applied. Images of PDO only and PDO/NK cell co-cultures (four to five technical replicates per condition) were acquired every 2–4 hours and analyzed using the SX5 IncuCyte software. First, PDOs were masked using brightfield images. Next, the Cytotox Red dye/hypoxia green dye signal within the PDO mask was quantified. Fold changes were calculated by dividing the red calibrated unit (RCU)/µm2 or green calibrated unit (GCU)/µm2 values of each time point by their values of the second measurement time point.

sec.title: Bulk RNA sequencing and analysis
sec.p: NK cells only and NK cell/PDO co-cultures were seeded in BME domes, cultured for 4 days at 37°C, digested, and sorted for live CD3−, CD56+, and EPCAM− cells as described above. RNA was isolated using the RNeasy Mini Kit (Qiagen) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. RNA libraries were prepared with the NEBNext Ultra II Directional RNA Library Prep Kit (New England BioLabs) with previous enrichment of messenger RNA (mRNA) using the NEBNext Poly(A) mRNA Magnetic Isolation Module (New England BioLabs), both according to the manufacturer’s instructions. The libraries were sequenced 150 bp single-end on an Illumina NextSeq 550 instrument (Illumina). Bulk RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) data were analyzed as previously described.39

Pathway responsive gene and transcription factor analyses were performed with the PROGENy (V.1.17.3)40 and DoRothEA packages (V.1.14.1).41 Heatmaps were created using the ggplot2 package (V.3.5.1) and ComplexHeatmap (V.2.18.0); expression values were normalized using z-score. The pathway analyses were carried out with the fgsea package and the enrichment browser package in R using the pathway information from the Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) database (https://www.genome.jp /kegg/pathway.html), or with the Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (GSEA) software (V.4.3.2).42 43 Because of the small sample size, the permutation type in the GSEA software was set to gene set. The hallmark hypoxia and other hypoxia-related pathways were extracted from the Molecular Signature Database.43 44 We received the analysis of TGF-β-mediated upregulated and downregulated transcripts in NK cells45 and extracted the top 100 downregulated transcripts (NK cell TGF-β signature). We applied the following published gene sets/signatures: NK cells at 1% O221 (top 40 upregulated transcripts in NK cells cultured at 1% O2 when compared with NK cell culture at 21% O2) and the tissue and blood score.46 All publicly available cytokines and chemokines were filtered for logFC values >1 and adjusted p values<0.05. To validate the NK cell/PDO co-culture-derived gene signatures, we downloaded the single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) data of NK cells from CRC tissues and peripheral blood27 (http://pan-nk.cancer-pku.cn/, peripheral blood: n=455 and tumor: n=368), pre-computed rankings of gene expression per cell and performed AUCell scoring (V.1.24.0)47 using custom gene sets with z-score normalization of NK cell gene expression values. Min-max normalization was subsequently applied to the area under the curve (AUC) scores across all cells. All transcripts of our NK cell/PDO co-culture-derived gene signatures and the respective cut-offs for signature curation are listed in (online supplemental table 3).

sec.title: Generation of gene-edited NK cells
sec.p: Isolated NK cells were cultured for 5–7 days with 400 U/mL IL-2, 10 ng/mL IL-15 (PeproTech), and 2,000 U/mL IL-1β (MBL). sgRNA duplexes were formed with CRISPR-RNA sequence (crRNA) and an ATTO-550 dye (IDT)-labeled transactivating-CRISPR RNA sequence (tracrRNA). 90 pmol of each RNA sequence was incubated for 5 min at 95°C in Duplex Buffer (IDT) and cooled down for 10 min at RT. 60 pmol of Cas9 ribonucleoprotein 2 NLS (Synthego) was prepared, incubated at RT for 20–60 min with sgRNA duplex and added to 1–2 million NK cells in 100 µL of Buffer T (Thermo Fisher). Electroporation was performed using a Neon Transfection System device (Thermo Fisher) applying one pulse of 1,900 volts during 20 ms, as previously described.48 The following crRNA guides were used: HIF1A ACAGTAACCAACCTCAGTGT (IDT), EPAS1 ACTGATTGGTTACCACCCTG (IDT), and Alt-R CRISPR-Cas9 negative control crRNA (computationally confirmed Alt-R CRISPR-Cas9 Negative Control crRNA, IDT). After electroporation, NK cells were resuspended in antibiotic-free media supplemented with 400 U/mL IL-2. HIF1A-edited/EPAS1-edited NK cells were sorted as CD3−CD56+ cells within the first 24 hours post-electroporation, according to ATTO-550 (IDT) expression.

The gene knockdown efficiency was determined by DNA sequencing (Eurofins). Total DNA was isolated using AllPrep DNA/RNA/Protein Kit (Qiagen) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. PCR was run using 50 ng DNA, 10 µL 5× HF PCR buffer (Thermo Fisher), 1 µL 10 mM dNTPs (each) (Thermo Fisher), 2.5 µL 100 µm primers (each), and 1 µL 2 U/µL Phusion Polymerase (Thermo Fisher). The following primers were used: HIF1A ACTAGCCGAGGAAGAACTATG and AGATGGGGTTTCACCACATTG and EPAS1: GCTTGATGTAGCAACTGGAG and GGTTCTTGGAGAACAGACATATG. Afterward, gel electrophoresis was performed, respective PCR bands were cut, and DNA was isolated using the QIAquick Gel Extraction Kit (Qiagen) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. 200 ng DNA was sequenced (Eurofins) using the following primers: HIF1A ATGTTGAAACATAGTCATCAGTG and EPAS1 GGTTCTTGGAGAACAGACATATG. The knockdown efficiency was calculated using tracking of indels by DEcomposition (TIDE) analysis.49

sec.title: Generation of B2M-edited PDO7
sec.p: The B2M knockout PDO7 line was generated by lentiviral transduction of PDO7 with LentiCRISPRv2 plasmid (Addgene, 52961). Guide RNA sequences were cloned into LentiCRISPRv2 according to a previously published study.50 LentiCIRSPRv2 plasmids were packaged into a lentiviral particle using plasmids pMD2G (Addgene, 12259) and psPAX2 (Addgene, 12260). The following guide RNA sequences were used sg_Luc: ACAACTTTACCGACCGCGCC, sg_hB2M: AGTCACATGGTTCACACGGC. B2M-negative cells were sorted according to human leukocyte antigen A, B, and C (HLA-ABC) expression.

sec.title: TCGA COAD expression and survival analysis
sec.p: First, we downloaded the fragments per kilobase of transcript per million mapped reads (FPKM) gene expression values as well as the clinical patient data from the colon adenocarcinoma (COAD) cohort collected in the Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA)51 using TCGAbiolinks (V.2.30.4). Next, we selected patients with primary tumors from whom both expression data as well as clinical data were available (n=456), and log2-transformed the FPKM gene expression values. We filtered patients for NCR1/KLRF1 expression >0, and patient-wise z-scores were calculated for each gene. Respective heatmaps were generated using pheatmap (V.1.0.12). For the correlation analyses, we used Pearson correlation, for the survival analysis, we selected patients with cancer in the top 25th and bottom 25th quartiles of respective gene expression and created Kaplan-Meier curves using survival (3.8–3) and survminer (0.5.0) (n=364 for NCR1 and n=380 for KLRF1). The corresponding p values were calculated using the log-rank test to assess differences in survival distributions between the two patient groups.

sec.title: Quantification of soluble factors
sec.p: Supernatants were collected after 4 days of NK cells only or NK cell/PDO co-cultures, spun down at 2,000 rpm for 10 min, and frozen at −80°C. On the day of measurement, supernatants were thawed on ice, spun down, and the concentrations of selected soluble factors were determined using a custom-made LEGENDplex panel (BioLegend) following the manufacturer’s instructions. Samples were analyzed using the LSRFortessa and the Qognit software (BioLegend).

sec.title: Statistics analysis
sec.p: For the calculation of the net NK cell-mediated killing of PDOs and the net increase of NK cell/PDO receptor expression or soluble factor secretion, respective values of PDO or NK cell only cultures were subtracted from the NK cell/PDO co-culture values. Prism V.10.2.3 (GraphPad) was used to analyze the data. Data sets were tested for normal distribution using the Shapiro-Wilk test, followed by paired or unpaired two-tailed t-test analysis, or one-way analysis of variance with Dunnett’s post hoc test (compared with NK cells only). For IncuCyte live-cell imaging, we applied AUC analysis, and in the case of correlation analyses, linear correlation using Pearson’s correlation coefficient. The significance was set at *p<0.05; **p<0.005; ***p<0.001; and ****p<0.0001. Blinding was not applied during the experiments or data collection, as procedures and analyses were conducted by the same investigator. Flow cytometry data analyses were performed unbiased, with consistent gating of lymphocyte populations.

sec.title: Differential susceptibility of CRC patient-derived organoids to NK cell-mediated killing
sec.p: To determine the efficacy of NK cells against CRC cells from individual patients, we established a co-culture platform of CRC PDO lines36 and human NK cells from buffy coats of healthy individuals (figure 1A). Our PDO platform includes eight PDO lines, categorized as CMS2 or CMS3 (online supplemental figure 1A). The PDO lines were established from biopsies collected from different locations along the intestinal tract and reflect the mutational landscape of CRC, including truncating mutations in APC, activating mutations in KRAS, and loss of TP53 (online supplemental figure 1A and online supplemental table 1). On co-culture with NK cells, we observed differential PDO susceptibilities to NK cell-mediated killing (figure 1B and online supplemental figure 1B-C). Compared with PDO13, PDO22, and PDO324, in co-culture with NK cells, PDO7, PDO19, PDO30, PDO46, and PDO330 displayed higher frequencies of apoptotic EPCAM+ tumor cells, indicative of higher NK cell-mediated killing. For simplification, according to the proportions of detected apoptotic cells in co-cultures, we defined PDOs as “NK cell-resistant” (<25% apoptotic tumor cells) and “NK cell-susceptible” (>25% apoptotic tumor cells). The stratification parameter was defined based on the susceptibility of the PDOs to NK cell-mediated killing using the cut-off of one quarter (25%). As representatives of NK cell-susceptible and NK cell-resistant PDOs, we selected PDO7 and PDO22. Of note, frequencies of NK cell-mediated PDO killing were not solely determined by the characteristics of the PDOs, but were also influenced by NK cell donor-specific differences in NK cell cytotoxicity (online supplemental figure 1D). Live-cell imaging confirmed a continuous increase in PDO7 cell death measured after labeling with Cytotox Red dye in co-culture with NK cells, whereas frequencies of dead cells within NK cell/PDO22 co-cultures remained unchanged over time (figure 1C–D and online supplemental figure 1E). To determine the impact of the PDO 3D structure on NK cell-mediated killing, we compared co-cultures of NK cells with PDOs cultured in 2D (single cells) and 3D. Frequencies of dead tumor cells from PDOs cultured in 2D were higher than their 3D counterparts, suggesting an impact of the 3D structure on NK cell responses (figure 1E). Taken together, we established an NK cell/PDO co-culture platform to monitor NK cell/PDO interactions, which detects differential patient-specific susceptibilities of individual PDOs to NK cell-mediated killing.

sec.title: PDO-exposed NK cells display TGF-β- and hypoxia-related signatures and a reduced expression of cytotoxicity-related transcripts
sec.p: To elucidate the impact of NK cell-susceptible or NK cell-resistant PDO environments on NK cells, we performed bulk transcriptome profiling (RNA-seq) of NK cells cultured for 4 days with PDO7 or PDO22 and compared them to NK cells cultured alone (figure 2A). Irrespective of exposure to NK cell-susceptible or NK cell-resistant PDOs, common transcriptional programs were enriched in NK cells after co-culture, including pathways related to hypoxia and TGF-β, when compared with NK cells cultured alone, whereas programs related to NFκB were only enriched in NK cells derived from co-cultures with NK cell-susceptible PDO7 (figure 2B and online supplemental figure 2A). To determine whether PDOs constitute hypoxic environments, we added the Image-iT hypoxia green dye, an enzymatically activatable dye that emits green fluorescence at an oxygen concentration below 5%. Indeed, both PDOs exhibited green fluorescent signals when analyzed using live-cell imaging (online supplemental figure 2B), indicative of a hypoxic PDO environment. GSEA against hypoxia-related pathways, as well as against a signature that we derived from human NK cells cultured for 7 days in 1% O2 in vitro,21 corroborated a significant enrichment in NK cells co-cultured with PDOs (figure 2C and online supplemental figure 2C-D). To test if PDO-induced effects relate to NK cells from patients with CRC, we generated an NK cell/PDO co-culture-specific hypoxia-related signature (online supplemental table 3), which we aligned with publicly available NK cell scRNA-seq data derived from blood and CRC tissues of patients.27 Indeed, CRC tissue-derived, but not blood-derived NK cells from patients with CRC, exhibited a high enrichment score in NK cell/PDO co-culture-derived hypoxia signatures (figure 2D). Next, we compared co-cultures of NK cells and PDOs cultured in normoxic (21% O₂) to those in hypoxic (1% O₂) conditions, revealing no significant differences in NK cell-mediated PDO killing. These data indicate that PDO-induced hypoxic environments might mimic conditions of 1% oxygen tension often observed in solid tumors (online supplemental figure 2E).

sec.p: To identify and predict activities of transcription factors regulating transcriptomic programs in PDO-exposed NK cells, we performed regulon-based scoring on our transcriptome data, using DoRothEA41 analysis. Our analysis predicted the transcriptional activities of NF-κB, TCF4, MYC, and RELA, as well as HIF-1α and EPAS1 (HIF-2α), transcription factors active in hypoxic environments,20 in NK cells derived from co-cultures with both NK cell-susceptible and NK cell-resistant PDOs (online supplemental figure 2F). To determine their functional role in NK cells, we disrupted either HIF1A or EPAS1 or both HIF1A/EPAS1 in primary NK cells using CRISPR-Cas9 technology, and confirmed allele targeting efficiencies by Sanger sequencing (online supplemental figure 2G). Compared with mock-treated NK cells, HIF1A/EPAS1-edited NK cells or NK cells with EPAS1 knockdown induced higher apoptosis rates in PDO7 and PDO22, while targeting of HIF1A resulted in an increase in NK cell-mediated killing of PDO7 (figure 2E and online supplemental figure 2H). Thus, exposure of NK cells to hypoxic environments present in PDO co-cultures induced hypoxia-inducible factors HIF1A/EPAS1, whose CRISPR-Cas9 mediated knockdown enhanced NK cell-mediated PDO killing.

In addition to the hypoxia pathway, the TGF-β pathway was enriched in NK cells following PDO exposure (figure 2B). To predict if NK cells exposed to PDOs indeed respond to TGF-β, we first obtained the human NK cell-specific TGF-β-response signature from published data,45 which demonstrated that the majority of significantly regulated transcripts were downregulated in NK cells on exposure to TGF-β. We have used this transcript set to perform GSEA on our data and revealed negative enrichment of these TGF-β-regulated transcripts in PDO-exposed NK cells compared with NK cells cultured alone (figure 2F). These findings support the hypothesis that PDOs constitute TGF-β-rich environments. We then narrowed the TGF-β-responsive gene set down to transcripts affected in our NK cell/PDO co-culture, thus generating an NK cell/PDO co-culture-specific TGF-β signature (online supplemental table 3). When applied on NK cells from the scRNA-seq data set of patients with CRC,27 this signature displayed lower enrichment score in CRC tissue-derived NK cells compared with peripheral blood NK cells (figure 2G). Ultimately, this indicates that perturbations in gene expression identified in NK cells exposed to TGF-β can be observed in NK cells derived from co-cultures with PDOs, as well as in NK cells from CRCs. To determine the impact of TGF-β on NK cell cytotoxicity towards PDOs, we applied galunisertib, a small molecule compound inhibiting TGF-βR1.52 compared with control conditions, in the presence of galunisertib, we observed enhanced NK cell-mediated killing of the majority of PDOs tested (figure 2H). Alongside, the addition of galunisertib reduced frequencies of CD103, an integrin regulated by TGF-β,23 expressing NK cells on co-culture with all PDOs tested (online supplemental figure 2I).

We next performed KEGG pathway analyses, focusing on the subcategory “Immune system”. In line with a previous publication analyzing various scRNA-seq NK cell data sets,27 we detected common depletion of “Natural Killer cell-mediated cytotoxicity pathway” regardless of whether NK cells were co-cultured with PDO7 or PDO22 (figure 2I). Based on downregulated transcripts, we then derived an NK cell/PDO co-culture-specific cytotoxicity signature (online supplemental table 3) that we overlaid with publicly available datasets27 and found a lower enrichment score in NK cells derived from CRC tissue compared with blood (figure 2J). In contrast, “IL-17 signaling” and “hematopoietic cell lineage” pathways were only enriched in NK cells co-cultured with NK cell-susceptible PDO7, but not NK cell-resistant PDO22 (figure 2I).

Taken together, our data indicate that NK cells from both NK cell-susceptible and NK cell-resistant PDO co-cultures displayed enriched TGF-β-related and hypoxia-related signatures, and both TGF-β and hypoxia-inducible factors EPAS1/HIF-1α impaired NK cell anti-PDO reactivity. TGF-β-related, hypoxia-related and NK cell cytotoxicity-related signatures in PDO-exposed NK cells aligned with those of NK cells derived from tissues of patients with CRC, supporting that PDO/NK cell co-cultures represent relevant models to study solid CRC microenvironments.

sec.title: NK cell-susceptible PDOs induce inflammatory transcriptional programs in NK cells
sec.p: As shown in (figure 2I), immune-related KEGG pathway analysis revealed an enrichment of the “IL-17 signaling” pathway. To create an NK cell inflammation signature, we extracted respective differentially expressed transcripts and included differentially regulated chemokines and cytokines53 revealing an upregulation of interferon (IFN)-γ, IL-1β, IL-13, CXCL1, or CCL20 in NK cells exposed to the NK cell-susceptible PDO7, but not to the NK cell-resistant PDO22 (figure 3A). We analyzed secretion of respective soluble factors in our whole PDO cohort, revealing that in concordance with the transcriptomics data, the proteins IFN-γ and IL-13 were detected at higher concentration in NK cell co-cultures with NK cell-susceptible PDOs compared with NK cell-resistant PDOs (figure 3B). Higher amounts of CXCL1 were present in NK cell co-cultures with NK cell-susceptible PDO7 and PDO30, when compared with respective PDO only cultures, while CCL20 was mainly produced by PDOs (online supplemental figure 3A).

sec.p: Of note, IL-1β was not detectable in our NK cell/PDO co-cultures (data not shown). Next, we curated an NK cell/PDO7 co-culture-specific NK cell inflammation signature (online supplemental table 3) that we overlaid with publicly available datasets27 and observed a higher enrichment score in NK cells from CRC tissues, when compared with peripheral blood (figure 3C). We also detected a positive correlation of the NK cell/PDO7 co-culture-specific inflammation signature with the expression of NK cell receptor transcripts NCR1 and KLRF1 in the COAD cohort (figure 3D),51 indicating that in patients with CRC, inflammatory “hot” TMEs, similar to our co-culture, might coincide with the presence of NK cells. In conclusion, our data demonstrate that on encounter of NK cell-susceptible PDOs, NK cells develop an inflammatory program characterized by expression of cytokines and chemokines characteristic of inflammation signatures in the TME in patients with CRC.

sec.title: NK cell-susceptible PDOs drive diversification of NK cell activation states and tissue-residency programs
sec.p: Among pathways predicted active in NK cells from NK cell-susceptible (PDO7), but not NK cell-resistant (PDO22) PDO co-cultures, we next focused on the “hematopoietic cell lineage” pathway (figure 2I), comprising transcripts IL2A (encoding CD25) and ITGA1 (encoding the activation/tissue-residency marker CD49a31 32) (figure 4A). In concordance with the transcriptomics data, we observed higher frequencies of CD25-expressing and CD49a-expressing NK cells in co-culture with NK cell-susceptible PDO lines compared with—resistant PDOs (figure 4B–C and online supplemental figure 4A-B). Upregulation of CD25 and CD49a on NK cells required direct contact with PDOs (online supplemental figure 4C). Downregulation of CD16 cell surface expression—commonly observed following NK cell activation54—was visible in NK cells exposed to NK cell-susceptible PDOs, while co-culture with—resistant PDOs did not induce CD16 downregulation on NK cells (figure 4B–C). Frequencies of CD25-expressing, CD49a-expressing, and CD16-negative cells positively correlated with proportions of NK cell-mediated PDO death (online supplemental figure 4D). Next, we generated the PDO7 co-culture-specific “hematopoietic cell lineage” signature (online supplemental table 3). After overlay with publicly available datasets,27 we observed a higher enrichment score in NK cells derived from patient with CRC tissues compared with peripheral blood NK cells (figure 4D). In line, there was a positive correlation of the NK cell/PDO7 co-culture-specific hematopoietic cell lineage signature with the expression of NK cell receptor transcripts NCR1 and KLRF1 in the COAD cohort (online supplemental figure 4E).51 t-SNE plots of CD25, CD49, and CD16 expression patterns revealed that NK cells exposed to NK cell-susceptible PDOs comprised CD16− and CD16+ NK cell subsets expressing either CD25 or CD49a or both, while the majority of NK cells cultured alone or with NK cell-resistant PDOs were CD16± CD25−CD49a− (figure 4E–F). These data indicate that NK cells can diversify into subsets with variable expression of CD25, CD49a, and CD16 on encounter with NK cell-susceptible PDOs. Moreover, in co-culture with NK cell-susceptible PDO7, expression of the activating receptor NKG2D, proportions of NK cells expressing the NK cell activation marker human leukocyte antigen (HLA)-DR,55 and inhibitory receptor NKG2A was increased compared with NK cells exposed to PDO22. Expression of T cell immunoreceptor with Ig and ITIM domains (TIGIT) and frequencies of TIM-3-expressing and CD96-expressing NK cells were more pronounced on NK cells from PDO7 co-cultures compared with PDO22 (online supplemental figure 4F). Frequencies of NK cells expressing the activation marker CD69 did not differ (online supplemental figure 4G). Moreover, we observed a higher proportion of NK cells expressing the chemokine receptor CXCR631 32 on co-culture with PDO7 compared with PDO22, while frequencies of CXCR3-expressing NK cells56 derived from both PDO7 and PDO22 co-cultures were comparably lower than NK cells cultured alone, suggesting receptor engagement, consistent with the presence of its ligand CXCL10 in these co-cultures (online supplemental figure 4H).57

sec.p: CD49a and CXCR6, implied as NK cell tissue-residency markers,31 32 were induced on co-culture with NK cell-susceptible PDO7, but not with NK cell-resistant PDO22. Thus, we determined scores of tissue-residency programs in PDO7-exposed or PDO22-exposed NK cells using a previously curated tissue score.46 58 GSEA revealed that in contrast to NK cells exposed to NK cell-resistant PDO22, only in PDO7-activated NK cells, gene set mirroring tissue-residency traits was significantly enriched (figure 4G). Accordingly, when applying the previously curated blood score,46 we observed a negative, significant enrichment score only in NK cells exposed to NK cell-susceptible PDO7 (figure 4G). These data indicate that NK cells exposed to the NK cell-susceptible PDO7 acquired features related to tissue residency. To determine the relevance of our findings to patients with CRC, we generated the NK cell/PDO7 co-culture-specific tissue and blood signatures (online supplemental table 3) and applied them to the previously described scRNA-seq dataset27 revealing a higher tissue and lower blood enrichment score in NK cells from CRC tissues compared with blood NK cells (figure 4H). In line, we detected a positive correlation of the NK cell/PDO7 co-culture-specific tissue signature with the combined expression of NCR1 and KLRF1 in the COAD cohort (online supplemental figure 4I).51
In summary, our data show that the encounter of NK cell-susceptible PDOs leads to phenotypic diversification of NK cells and drives transcriptional signatures related to tissue residency.

sec.title: NK cell-susceptible PDOs display MICA/Bhigh and MHC class Ilow phenotypes
sec.p: So far, our data indicated that cell–cell contact between NK cells and PDOs was critical for high frequencies of CD25-expressing and CD49a-expressing NK cells on exposure to NK cell-susceptible PDOs (online supplemental figure 4C). To determine the expression of proteins that can interact with inhibitory or activating receptors on NK cells, we performed flow cytometric analysis of PDOs. HLA-ABC, ligands for inhibitory KIRs, were expressed by all PDOs, except PDO19 (figure 5A). All PDOs expressed the nectin-like molecules CD112 and CD155 (ligands for the activating receptor DNAM-1 and inhibitory receptors TIGIT/CD96). NK cell-susceptible PDOs, but not NK cell-resistant PDOs, were distinguished by the expression of MHC class I polypeptide-related sequence A and B (MICA/B), ligands of the activating NK cell receptor NKG2D, whereas PDO46 differed by higher expression of the death receptors FAS and TNF-related apoptosis-inducing ligand receptor 2 (TRAIL-R2), compared with other PDOs, consistent with susceptibility to NK cell-mediated killing. Of note, B7-H6 (ligand for NKp30), programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-L1), TRAIL-R1, and HLA-DR were not detectable on PDOs (data not shown). Taken together, despite the heterogeneous expression of ligands for NK cell receptors on PDOs, we could distinguish NK cell-susceptible and NK cell-resistant PDOs by MICA/B, death receptor ligand, and high MHC class I expression, respectively.

sec.p: Expression of HLA-ABC and MICA/B negatively and positively correlated with proportions of apoptotic PDOs in NK cell co-cultures, respectively (online supplemental figure 5A). To determine the involvements of HLA-ABC and MICA/B in NK cell-mediated PDO killing, we generated B2M-deficient PDO7, lacking MHC class I expression (online supplemental figure 5B), or abrogated NKG2D engagement using a blocking mAb. Compared with controls, we detected higher frequencies of apoptotic B2M-deficient PDO7 in NK cell co-cultures indicating that lack of MHC class I expression on PDOs enhanced the susceptibility of PDOs to NK cells (figure 5B). Moreover, compared with control mAb, we observed a lower proportion of apoptotic MICA/B-expressing PDOs (PDO7, PDO30, and PDO330) in the presence of anti-NKG2D blocking mAbs revealing an involvement of the MICA/B/NKG2D axis, while NK cell-mediated killing of PDO22, a PDO with no detectable MICA/B expression, was low regardless of the addition of the anti-NKG2D blocking mAbs (figure 5C). To test whether these pathways also impacted NK cell phenotypes, we analyzed NK cells by flow cytometry on co-culture with several NK cell-susceptible and NK cell-resistant PDOs. Compared with controls, in the absence of HLA-ABC on PDOs, co-cultured NK cells expressed more CD25, CD49a, and less CD16, while in the absence of NKG2D engagement, NK cells expressed less CD25, CD49a, and more CD16, respectively (figure 5D–E), suggesting a contribution of both MHC class I and MICA/B on PDOs in shaping the diversification of activation states in NK cells. Since MICA expression marked NK cell-susceptible PDOs, we set out to determine the relevance of MICA expression in patient samples from The Cancer Genome Atlas datasets (figure 5F).51 We detected a positive correlation of MICA expression with the expression of the NK cell-associated transcripts NCR1/KLRF1. Moreover, the NCR1/MICAhigh signature correlated with a better overall patient with CRC survival when compared with the NCR1/MICAlow signature in the COAD cohort. These data suggest that mechanisms determining PDO susceptibility to NK cell-mediated killing identified by our study might also operate in patients with CRC. Furthermore, we identified a potential prognostic role of the NCR1/MICAhigh signature in patients with CRC.

NK cell transfers together with antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity (ADCC)-engaging mAbs represent a promising strategy to enhance NK cell antitumor reactivities.59 Thus, in our PDO/NK cell co-cultures, we tested an ADCC-inducing mAb (CM24) against CEACAM1, a carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA)-related cell adhesion molecule, that is, also detectable in COAD,60 expressed by both NK cell-resistant and NK cell-susceptible PDOs (figure 5G). Addition of anti-CEACAM1 mAb increased proportions of apoptotic PDOs in NK cell co-cultures with NK cell-resistant PDO22, to a lesser extent in co-cultures with NK cell-susceptible PDO330, but not in co-cultures with PDO7 and PDO30 (figure 5H). Compared with controls, in the presence of anti-CEACAM1 mAb, we detected higher proportions of CD25-expressing and CD49a-expressing NK cells, and lower frequencies of CD16-expressing NK cells from both NK cell-susceptible and NK cell-resistant PDO co-cultures (figure 5I). Of note, before the addition of the anti-CEACAM1 mAb, frequencies of CD16-expressing NK cells from co-cultures with NK cell-susceptible PDO7 were lower compared with NK cells from co-cultures with—resistant PDOs (figure 5I), which might explain why the addition of CAECAM-1 mAb to PDO7/NK cell co-cultures did not affect PDO death. However, despite low CD16 expression, CD16 expression appeared sufficient for the anti-CEACAM1 mAb to mediate NK cell activation in both NK cell/PDO co-cultures.

Taken together, our results revealed that PDOs can be divided into NK cell-susceptible PDOs by MICA/Bhigh and death receptor (FAS/TRAIL-R2)high expression, as well as NK cell-resistant PDOs by MHC class Ihigh expression, and highlights the potential of our NK cell/PDO platform for the testing of therapeutic mAbs.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: PDOs provide innovative tools enabling the assessment of the intertumoral heterogeneity of solid cancers. Accordingly, previous studies highlighting the relevance of PDO/immune cell co-cultures for preclinical testing of immunotherapeutic strategies focused on T cells61 62 or on the NK cell line NK92, harnessed by a chimeric antigen receptor (CAR).38 63 To decipher NK cell reactivities against CRCs derived from individual patients, we established a co-culture model of PDOs from colon cancer biopsies36 with primary allogeneic human NK cells. Although we observed differential patient-specific susceptibilities of individual PDOs to NK cell-mediated killing, we could divide the whole PDO cohort into NK cell-susceptible and NK cell-resistant PDOs. NK cell-susceptible PDOs were efficiently killed by NK cells and could also drive NK cell activation and tissue-residency programs, highlighting the potential for NK cell-based therapies for this patient with CRC group. Accordingly, our platform may support the pre-selection of patients who could benefit from NK cell-based immunotherapies. For preclinical evaluation of NK cell-based therapies, the inclusion of matched non-tumor organoids would be valuable to assess potential off-tumor cytotoxicity. However, our protocol for generating PDOs from small biopsy samples of patients with CRC did not yield matched non-tumor tissues due to limited tissue availability. In our NK cell/PDO co-culture system, NK cells were of allogeneic origin and not HLA/KIR matched. Several studies indicate that HLA/KIR mismatch potentiates NK cell-mediated cytotoxicity due to “missing self-recognition” and on adoptive NK cell transfer is associated with improved survival in patients with hematologic malignancies.64 65 In addition, expression of MICA/B, ligands for the activating receptor NKG2D, correlated with enhanced susceptibility of PDOs to NK cell-mediated killing. These MICA/B expressing PDOs might also elicit effective killing by autologous NK cell products that are currently discussed for clinical applications.66

PDO/immune cell co-culture models can provide valuable insights into how exposure of immune cells to solid TMEs affects immune cell behaviors in a patient-specific manner.67 In solid tumors, immune cells face a hostile microenvironment15 whose complexity remains challenging to model in the human system. Although our NK cell/PDO co-cultures lacked important components of the CRC microenvironment, such as fibroblasts and myeloid cells, transcriptome analysis of PDO-exposed NK cells revealed communalities with NK cells extracted from patient with CRC tissues.27 Similar to NK cells derived from CRC tissues, TGF-β-related and hypoxia-related pathways were among the highest enriched transcriptional programs in PDO-exposed NK cells, irrespective of the PDO tested. TGF-β suppresses NK cell functions including proliferation, cytotoxicity, cytokine production, and cell adhesion.22 23 Its receptor, TGF-βR1, is targeted in current clinical trials (NCT02423343, NCT02734160, NCT01246986, NCT01722825, and NCT02688712) across different solid tumors using the inhibitor galunisertib, which could also increase NK cell-mediated PDO killing in our co-culture system. More recently, deletion of the transcription factor SMAD4 in NK cells downstream of TGF-βR was reported as an effective strategy to enhance NK cell antitumor activity.23 We propose that our platform, mimicking TGF-β-rich environments, could be of relevance for preclinical testing of such compounds and cell products.

Many solid tumors are characterized by low oxygen concentration, reaching below 1%.68 Hypoxia was reported to reduce cellular function, such as proliferation, cytotoxicity, and the expression of activating receptors on human NK cells.19,21 In concordance with previous data,61 using a hypoxia-sensitive dye, we detected oxygen concentrations in PDOs to be below 5%, and therefore postulate that our co-culture model might be valuable for studying the impact of hypoxia on immune cell function in a 3D setting. We further substantiated this hypothesis by demonstrating that NK cell-mediated PDO killing remained largely unchanged in co-cultures under hypoxic conditions (1% O2), suggesting that PDO-induced hypoxia recapitulates the low oxygen tensions typically found in solid tumors. In PDO-exposed NK cells, the hypoxia-inducible factors HIF1A and EPAS1 (HIF-2α) were among the top positively associated transcription factors. Although HIF-2α and HIF-1α share a high degree of similarity, they differ in expression patterns and structure and regulate expression of overlapping as well as distinct target genes.69 Both HIF-1α and HIF-2α have been implicated in cytotoxic T-cell responses to hypoxia.70 71 In the context of T regulatory cells (Tregs), HIF-2α repressed HIF-1α expression, suggesting a crosstalk between HIF-1α and HIF-2α.72 Deletion of Hif1α in murine NK cells reduced tumor growth in certain mouse models.19 26 73 Although a previous study using NK cell-specific Epas1 KO mice concluded that HIF-2α does not affect NK cell homeostasis and activation in vitro,74 the in vivo role of HIF-2α in mouse tumor models or human NK cells was not addressed. In our experimental system, knockdown of either HIF1A or EPAS1, or both, in human NK cells resulted in an enhanced NK cell-mediated PDO killing, with variable degrees across PDOs. Focusing on testing the cytotoxic activity of HIF-1α-deficient NK cells against ovarian carcinoma target cells, a recent study obtained similar results.21 It is possible that certain features of PDOs, including concentrations of O2 or the expression of inflammatory cytokines/chemokines, might impact the reactivity of HIF1A/EPAS1-edited NK cells. Future studies should address the potential of combination therapies to enhance the antitumor activity of HIF1A/EPAS1-edited NK cells.

In addition to NK cell adaptations that were independent of PDO susceptibility, our study also revealed PDO patient-specific NK cell characteristics, including highly diverse NK cell responses in NK cell co-cultures with NK cell-susceptible PDOs. NK cell-susceptible PDOs induced gene profiles associated with inflammation in NK cells, characterized by secretion of cytokines such as IFN-γ and IL-13, aligning with data from NK cells derived from CRC tissues.27 33 Moreover, on encounter of NK cell-susceptible, and not NK cell-resistant PDOs, we observed the appearance of diverse NK cell phenotypes, whereby CD16+ and CD16− populations differentially expressed CD25 and/or CD49a. CD49a and CXCR6, both markers of human tissue-resident NK cells,31 32 were induced in NK cells exposed to NK cell-susceptible PDOs, whereas CD103 and integrin involved in tissue residency upregulated by TGF-β23 were induced in response to both PDO7 and PDO22. Noteworthy, we observed that only PDO-activated NK cells showed a significant enrichment of a previously published tissue score,46 while we detected simultaneous depletion of transcripts associated with a blood score.46 It is important to note that our setup does not allow the investigation of bona fide tissue-resident NK cells31 but can serve as a model studying blood-derived NK cells entering the tumor tissues.

In our study, exposure of allogeneic blood-derived NK cells to PDOs shaped NK cell phenotypic and transcriptional states. This included activation and inflammatory profiles together with the acquisition of tissue-residency traits corresponding to signatures derived from NK cells in CRC tissues reported by Tang et al.27 Recently, Rebuffet et al30 determined the distribution patterns of NK cell subsets one to three in human tissues and in 22 cancer types including CRC, revealing the presence of all three NK cell subsets, enriched in canonical CD56dim, canonical CD56bright and human cytomegalovirus-driven adaptive NK cells, respectively, in the CRC tissue. Further analyses are needed to determine how signatures derived from our study would correspond to NK1-3 subsets as defined by Rebuffet et al.30

PDOs showed a heterogeneity in the expression of ligands that interact with activating and inhibiting NK cell receptors. We observed that HLA-ABClow (ligands for inhibitory KIRs) and MICA/Bhigh (ligands for the activating receptor NKG2D) profiles marked NK cell-susceptible PDOs. CRCs are reported to frequently display MHC class Ilow phenotypes, possibly to escape from CD8+ T-cell attack,75 highlighting high potential for NK cell-based therapies. Our data showed that patients with NCR1/KLRF1high and MICAhigh signatures have increased overall survival rates when compared with their low signature counterparts.76 In line, decreased NK cell numbers, as well as impaired NK cell functionality, both in CRC tissues and blood, correlated with poorer overall survival of patients with CRC.33 77

ADCC represents a potent NK cell effector function and has been identified as a key mechanism of action for therapeutic mAbs, such as rituximab (anti-CD20)78 or trastuzumab (anti-HER2).79 Hence, we tested an mAb (CM24) inducing ADCC, which was directed against CEACAM1, a CEA-related cell adhesion upregulated in COAD,60 reported to be associated with poor overall survival.80 Although anti-CAECAM1 mAb addition increased NK cell-mediated killing of PDO22, but not of the other PDOs tested, NK cell activation was markedly increased in NK cell co-cultures of all NK cell-susceptible as well as NK cell-resistant PDOs suggesting differential activation requirements for NK cell-mediated killing versus activation using anti-CAECAM1 mAbs. Noteworthy, CEACAM1 as a target for therapeutic mAbs is currently being tested in clinical trials (NCT02346955 and NCT04731467).

In conclusion, we show that our NK cell/PDO co-culture platform is able to identify both PDO patient-specific and patient-common effects on NK cell function, shedding light on the mechanisms underlying PDO susceptibility. Moreover, it enables us to capture diverse NK cell reactivities against CRCs of individual patients. Ultimately, we envisage that the NK cell/PDO platform could serve for preclinical testing of therapeutic mAbs and small molecular compounds in combination with cellular immunotherapies from different donors and sources, including (cord) blood-derived NK cells, induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived NK cells, or CAR-NK cells.
